points: Luigi Galvani, working in Bologna in the 1780s, found that a dissected frog's leg twitched when touched by two different metals at once.
Galvani believed the electricity came from the animal itself, which he called “animal electricity”.
Alessandro Volta showed that the electricity came from two different metals in contact with a conducting liquid.
In 1800 Volta built the first battery, the voltaic pile: a stack of zinc and copper (or silver) discs separated by cardboard or cloth soaked in salt water.
Galvanic cells, also called voltaic cells, are named after Galvani and Volta.

notes.h: How a redox reaction makes a current
points: When zinc is put directly into copper(II) sulfate solution, zinc atoms give electrons straight to Cu²⁺ ions: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s).
Copper is deposited, the blue colour fades and the energy is released as heat, with no useful current; this is a displacement reaction.
A galvanic cell separates the oxidation and the reduction into two half-cells, so the electrons must travel through an external wire from one to the other.
This flow of electrons is an electric current.
A half-cell is an electrode dipping into a solution of its own ions, e.g. zinc in zinc sulfate solution.

The metal higher in the electrochemical series (see "The electrochemical series and displacement"), the one more easily oxidised, becomes the anode (negative); the lower metal is the cathode (positive).
The further apart the two metals are in the electrochemical series, the greater the voltage of the cell.
Under standard conditions (1 M solutions, 25 °C) the cell voltages are: magnesium–copper 2.71 V; zinc–copper 1.10 V; iron–copper 0.78 V.

notes.b: The copper–zinc cell is the standard galvanic cell, with the zinc and copper in separate beakers joined by wires and a salt bridge.
points: Set-up: a zinc strip in 1 M zinc sulfate solution and a copper strip in 1 M copper(II) sulfate solution, in separate beakers.
The metals are joined by wires through a voltmeter or bulb, and the solutions by a salt bridge; the voltage is about 1.1 V.
Zinc electrode (anode, negative, oxidation): Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻. Zinc atoms lose electrons and go into solution as ions.
Copper electrode (cathode, positive, reduction): Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s). Copper(II) ions from the solution gain electrons and are deposited as copper.
Overall cell reaction: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), the same redox reaction as the direct displacement described above.
Zinc is the reducing agent and Cu²⁺ is the oxidising agent.
Electrons flow through the external wire from the zinc to the copper.
Over time the zinc electrode wears away and loses mass, while the copper electrode gains a fresh pink-brown coating and gains mass.
The blue colour of the copper(II) sulfate solution fades as Cu²⁺ is used up, and the voltage slowly falls.

notes.b: The salt bridge connects the two solutions without letting them mix.
points: A salt bridge is a strip of filter paper soaked in potassium nitrate (or potassium chloride) solution, or a U-tube of the salt solution set in agar gel.
It completes the circuit: ions move through it, carrying charge between the half-cells.
It keeps each solution electrically neutral: as Zn²⁺ ions build up in the zinc half-cell, negative ions (NO₃⁻) move into it.
As Cu²⁺ ions are removed from the copper half-cell, positive ions (K⁺) move into it.
Without it, charge would build up in each beaker and the current would stop at once.
Potassium nitrate is used because its ions do not react with the electrode solutions; it forms no precipitate.

notes.h: Practical: creating a simple galvanic cell
points: Aim: to build a copper–zinc galvanic cell, measure its voltage, and compare the voltages from different pairs of metals.

Variables: the independent variable is the pair of metals; the dependent variable is the voltage; the controlled variables are the concentration and volume of the solutions, the temperature, and the size and cleanliness of the strips.
1. Clean strips of zinc and copper with sandpaper (emery paper) to remove the oxide layer, which would otherwise reduce the voltage.
2. Half-fill one beaker with 1 M zinc sulfate solution and another with 1 M copper(II) sulfate solution; stand the zinc strip in the first and the copper strip in the second.
3. Soak a strip of filter paper in potassium nitrate solution and drape it between the two beakers, with each end in a solution.
4. Connect the metals to a voltmeter with leads and crocodile clips, zinc to the negative terminal, and record the voltage.
5. Replace the voltmeter with a small bulb or LED to show that a current flows.
6. Remove the salt bridge and record the voltage again; it falls to zero, showing the bridge is needed.
7. Repeat with other metal pairs, e.g. magnesium–copper and iron–copper, each metal in a solution of its own ions, using a fresh salt bridge each time.

notes.h: Practical: results, safety, errors and diagram
points: Results: the measured voltages are usually a little lower than the standard values, and the larger the gap between the metals in the electrochemical series, the larger the voltage.
A simpler cell: zinc and copper strips pushed into a lemon, or dipped into one beaker of salt solution or dilute acid, also give a voltage, because the juice or solution is an electrolyte.

Safety: wear goggles; copper(II) sulfate is harmful, an irritant and toxic to aquatic life, so do not pour it down the sink and dispose of it as directed; zinc sulfate is an irritant; wash hands afterwards.
Sources of error: an oxide layer left on the metals; solutions not exactly 1 M or not at 25 °C; the salt bridge drying out; the voltmeter drawing some current.

Diagram: two beakers, zinc in zinc sulfate and copper in copper(II) sulfate, joined by a potassium nitrate salt bridge, with wires from each metal to a voltmeter; label the anode (−) and cathode (+) and the direction of electron flow from zinc to copper.

keyTerms.definition: A cell in which a spontaneous redox reaction, split into two half-cells, drives electrons through an external circuit.
An electrode dipping into a solution of its own ions, forming one half of a galvanic cell.
A strip of filter paper or a U-tube of salt solution that joins two half-cells, letting ions flow to complete the circuit without the solutions mixing.
A galvanic cell with a zinc electrode in zinc sulfate and a copper electrode in copper(II) sulfate, giving about 1.1 V.
A reaction in which a more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in its compound, as zinc does with copper(II) ions.
The first battery, built by Volta in 1800 from stacked zinc and copper discs separated by cloth soaked in salt water.
A thin coating of oxide on a metal strip that must be removed by sanding, as it would otherwise lower the voltage of a cell.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would make a simple copper–zinc galvanic cell. Write the half-equation at each electrode, identify the anode and the cathode, and show the direction of electron flow.
questions.model: Clean a zinc strip and a copper strip with sandpaper to remove the oxide layer. Half-fill one beaker with 1 M zinc sulfate solution and place the zinc strip in it; half-fill a second beaker with 1 M copper(II) sulfate solution and place the copper strip in it. Soak a strip of filter paper in potassium nitrate solution to make a salt bridge, and drape it between the two beakers with each end in a solution. Connect the zinc and copper strips to a voltmeter with leads and crocodile clips, zinc to the negative terminal, and record the voltage, about 1.1 V. Zinc is oxidised at the anode, which is the negative electrode: Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻. Copper(II) ions are reduced at the cathode, which is the positive electrode: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s). Electrons flow through the external wire from the zinc electrode to the copper electrode. Inside the cell, ions move through the salt bridge to complete the circuit.

questions.prompt: State two functions of the salt bridge in a galvanic cell and name a suitable substance for it.
questions.model: First, it completes the circuit: ions move through the salt bridge, carrying charge between the two half-cells. Second, it keeps each solution electrically neutral: as Zn²⁺ ions build up in the zinc half-cell, negative ions move into it from the bridge, and as Cu²⁺ ions are removed from the copper half-cell, positive ions move into it from the bridge. A suitable substance is potassium nitrate solution soaked into a strip of filter paper, because its ions do not react with the electrode solutions.

questions.prompt: Explain why no current is produced when a zinc strip is placed directly in copper(II) sulfate solution, but a current flows when the two half-reactions are separated.
questions.model: When zinc is placed directly in copper(II) sulfate solution, zinc atoms transfer electrons straight to Cu²⁺ ions in the same beaker: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s). The electrons never pass through an external wire, so there is no current; the energy is released as heat and the blue colour fades. In a galvanic cell the two half-reactions are separated into two half-cells, so the electrons lost by zinc must travel through an external wire to reach the Cu²⁺ ions at the copper electrode. This flow of electrons is an electric current.
